nameStory: This lichen gets its name from its bumpy, wart-like appearance and its discovery in Texas, where it was first scientifically described. The warty texture comes from the rounded bumps (called verrucae) that house the lichen's reproductive structures, making the surface look like it's covered in tiny skin warts.
description: Texas Wart Lichen is a crusty, bark-dwelling lichen that forms patches directly on tree bark, almost like someone splattered thick paint that dried with bumps. It appears as grayish or whitish crusty patches decorated with distinctive rounded bumps or warts across the surface. These patches can spread several inches across the bark, creating an unmistakable bumpy texture that feels rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Warty surface texture
idTips.description: The surface is covered with distinct rounded bumps or warts that feel rough and gritty when you gently run your finger across them, like touching coarse sandpaper with pebbles glued on

idTips.label: Crusty bark growth
idTips.description: Forms tight, crusty patches that seem painted or glued directly onto tree bark, with no leafy edges or obvious separation from the bark surface

idTips.label: Grayish-white color
idTips.description: Overall grayish to whitish appearance, sometimes with a slightly greenish tint, similar to dried concrete or old paint

idTips.label: Bark-dwelling habit
idTips.description: Always found growing directly on tree bark, never on rocks or soil, with the lichen body firmly attached and difficult to peel off

habitat: Extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation, likely found on bark of deciduous or mixed forest trees in warmer, protected locations. Given its southwestern origin, any New England occurrence would probably be in the warmest microclimates, possibly in urban areas or southern-facing slopes where temperatures are moderated.

seasonality.spring: Most visible after winter moisture has cleaned the bark surface, making the grayish warty patches stand out clearly against fresh bark. The bumpy texture is most pronounced when slightly damp from spring rains.
seasonality.summer: Can appear dried out and less conspicuous during hot, dry periods, but the distinctive warty bumps remain the key identifying feature even when the lichen looks dusty or faded.
seasonality.fall: Often becomes more noticeable as leaves fall and expose more bark surface, and autumn moisture may enhance the lichen's color and make it easier to spot.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round since it's growing on bark, though may be partially obscured by snow or ice. Winter is actually a good time to search since there are fewer distractions and bark is fully exposed.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that there's only been one confirmed sighting in the entire region - it's like finding a cactus in a pine forest, since this species is naturally at home in the hot, dry Southwest and somehow made it all the way to New England!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other bumpy bark lichens like Rock Wart Lichen, but Texas Wart Lichen's bumps are more distinctly rounded and wart-like rather than irregularly shaped. Remember: if it looks like tiny skin warts scattered across the bark, you might have found this southwestern wanderer.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'Texas' in this lichen creates confusion since it's normally found in the Southwest, not New England - finding one here would be like discovering a piece of desert ecology that somehow traveled north, possibly through human transport of infected bark or unusual climate conditions.
compareHints: Texas Wart Lichen differs from its Pertusaria relatives by having more distinctly rounded, wart-like bumps compared to the irregular lumps of Rock Wart Lichen or the pustule-like swellings of Branch Bumps. Its southwestern origin also sets it apart from other New England Pertusaria species, which are adapted to cooler, moister northeastern conditions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rock Wart Lichen differs from its cousin Branch Bumps by growing exclusively on rock rather than tree bark, and from other Pertusaria species by its particularly thick, substantial crust and prominent warty structures.
Branch Bumps differs from its Pertusaria relatives primarily in its habitat preference for bark over rock and its particularly pronounced warty bumps.
Macoun's Wart Lichen differs from its Pertusaria relatives by having more prominent, well-defined warty bumps compared to the flatter Rock Wart Lichen or the more pustule-like Branch Bumps.
Unlike its more common relatives Rock Wart Lichen and Branch Bumps, this species shows distinctive reddish coloration rather than plain gray or white.
Unlike Rock Wart Lichen which forms obvious rounded bumps, or Branch Bumps which creates pustule-like growths, Pertusaria sulcata is distinguished by its grooved, furrowed surface texture.
